did_you_know.text: The chapter opens with a call to uphold justice and practice righteousness, because the LORD’s salvation is near and his righteousness is about to be revealed.
The blessing in this chapter is connected not only with keeping the Sabbath, but also with avoiding every kind of evil: “keeping his hand from doing any evil.”
The chapter also addresses the foreigner and the eunuch, making clear that they should not say they are separated from the LORD’s people or without hope before him.
Eunuchs who keep the Sabbath, choose what pleases the LORD, and hold fast to his covenant are promised a place and a memorial in the LORD’s house.
The expression “a name and a memorial” describes an everlasting name for the eunuchs that will not be cut off; it is even said to be better than sons and daughters.
Foreigners who join themselves to the LORD, love his name, serve him, keep the Sabbath, and hold fast to his covenant are presented as part of the community that worships the LORD.
The LORD’s house is called “a house of prayer for all nations”; the foreigners brought to his holy mountain will be able to pray and offer acceptable sacrifices on his altar.
Alongside his acceptance of foreigners, the LORD declares that he will gather the scattered people of Israel and will gather others to them as well.
In the second half of the chapter, the wild animals and animals of the forest are called to come and devour, portraying the people as exposed to danger.
The watchmen and leaders are described as blind and silent dogs who do not know, bark, or warn; later they are portrayed as greedy and drunk.
